item.title: Former US Vice President Mike Pence says ‘last thing we need right now…is a trade war with Canada’ as talks fail
item.description: Former US Vice President Mike Pence warns that the escalating US-Canada trade war could hurt Washington’s economy. His remarks follow Washington’s 50% tariffs on Canadian imports  worth $20 billion and Ottawa's plan to impose retaliatory tariffs from 8 September.
item.dc:creator: Swati Gandhi
item.content:encoded: Mike Pence, the former US Vice President who served under President Donald Trump from 2017 to 2021, warned on Sunday (local time) that escalating US-Canada trade poses new risks to Washington's economy. Speaking from the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, where he was attending the 35th anniversary of Ukraine’s independence, Pence said Americans are already struggling with high costs and urged negotiations over confrontation.Mike Pence calls for negotiations between US and CanadaPence told CNN, "We hear about the issue of affordability right now," and added, "I think the last thing we need right now, as our economy is getting back on its feet, is a trade war with Canada."The former VP said there has been "hot rhetoric" from both Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney. Pence said he hoped, for “the sake of American families,” that “what we’re looking at here is negotiation and not confrontation in a trade war.”He further said, “That’s how I would advise the president: Drive a hard bargain. But let’s pursue free trade with free nations, most especially our trading partners to the north."His remarks came days after the United States imposed 50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion worth of Canadian imports, including whisky and hockey gear, following the collapse of trade talks.Donald Trump takes dig at Canada after trade talks failTrump took a dig at Canada after negotiations with Ottawa failed. In a Truth Social post, on 22 August, he wrote, "Canada wants the benefits of being a State, without being one!!! They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of Tariffs. No more!!!"Trump made these remarks as Washington's 50% tariffs on Canadian imports were set to come into effect at 12:01 am on 22 August.Previously, the US president had expressed optimism about finalizing a deal with Canada and cited his good relationship with Carney. Trump had said that Washington “should be able to have a deal with Canada.”US imposes 50% tariffs on CanadaOn 21 August (local time), Washington announced 50% tariffs on Canadian goods, including plywood, liquor, electrical equipment and hockey gear, Bloomberg reported. The development came after the two countries had been negotiating for several weeks and had prepared a draft agreement proposing to lower tariffs on some Canadian steel and aluminium to 25% and reduce duties on Canadian automobiles to 15%.In return, Ottawa was expected to withdraw the retaliatory measures it introduced last year. Reports said the White House was seeking several concessions, including the removal of Canada's counter-tariffs on US vehicles and an end to restrictions on the retail sale of American alcoholic beverages in most Canadian provinces.Canada announces reciprocal tariffsFollowing the collapse of trade negotiations between the two long-standing allies, Carney announced retaliatory tariffs on US imports, saying he had rejected a "bad deal" as tensions between the countries continued to escalate.Carney said, "You're at war when you get attacked. We got attacked." He added, "In recent days, the United States proposed new terms that were uneconomic, unfair and undermined the net benefits for Canada, and called into question the reliability of any deal."He also said, "We cannot accept what they've offered, and we will not give what they've asked."The Canadian PM noted that one of the main reasons the deal fell through at the last minute was Washington's decision to impose restrictions on Canada's trade with other countries.He said Washington's negotiators had also made unacceptable "threats" to the French language and "Quebec culture", referring to the French-speaking province in eastern Canada.According to AFP, the Canadian PM said Ottawa's tariffs would target the US steel and dairy industries and take effect on 8 September. He added that further details would be announced next week.

item.title: Petrol and diesel prices today — 24 Aug: Check fuel rates in Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru, other cities as crude oil falls
item.description: Petrol and diesel prices today: Fuel rates in Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru and other cities stood steady even though oil prices eased on Monday. Check exact fuel rates in Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru and other cities here.
item.dc:creator: Fareha Naaz
item.content:encoded: Petrol and diesel prices today, 24 August: Fuel rates remained unchanged across major Indian cities on Monday as oil prices eased. Amid global energy crisis due to West Asia conflict, state-owned fuel retailers continue to shield consumers from oil price volatility and fluctuation.Fuel rates across major Indian cities recorded marginal changes as they are revised at 6:00 AM daily because India follows dynamic fuel price method. Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) last brought about major price revision on 25 May, since then fuel prices have been steady.Check latest petrol and diesel prices in your city on 24 August*Source: GoodreturnsCrude oil price todayOil prices slipped on Monday as investors await details of US sanctions on Iran which may further disrupt energy supplies from West Asia. The global benchmark Brent crude plunged 1.0% and traded around $93.43 a barrel 1.0% after gains of 6.6% last week while US crude slipped 1.1% to $86.14 a barrel, Reuters reported.US-Iran war news updateAmid US-Iran deadlock on peace talks, both contracts posted their second weekly gains last week and rose more than 5%. Due to continued US blockade of Iranian ports, oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz thinned which once handled 20% of global oil and gas supplies.US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is all set to hold a press conference at 2 pm EDT today following US President Donald Trump's economic pressure campaign threat for Tehran and its trading partners, including China.Vowing to severe all economic ties and isolate Iran, Scott Bessent in a post on X stated, “President Trump has dismantled Iran’s military capabilities, destroyed nearly 100 percent of its military factories, and buried its nuclear program. We are now entering the endgame. At dawn begins an economic D-Day — the single greatest financial offensive ever marshaled against an adversary.”According to trade sources, offers of Iranian crude to Chinese buyers have declined and prices jumped due to US blockade of Iran's shipments. As per Iran’s state news agency IRNA, Iraqi oil tankers were granted permission to transit through Hormuz following repeated requests.Commonwealth Bank of Australia commodities analyst, Vivek Dhar, said, “It is unclear whether US policy to economically isolate Iran will prove effective,” Reuters reported. He added, “But if the US measures do work as intended, Iran's ability to respond via increased violence becomes a growing risk for energy markets to consider.”Even as Tehran condemned Trump's new sanctions and called them ‘economic terrorism,' and ‘crimes against humanity’, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian pushed for a diplomatic solution.
